strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important failure mode (identity duplication/collapse and miscounting) in multi-human text-to-image generation that has been noted in prior work (e.g., MultiHuman-TestBench) but not directly targeted by an annotation-free training method.

The compositional reward design (intra-image diversity, group-wise cross-sample diversity via a leave-one-out counterfactual statistic, count accuracy, and HPS-based quality control) is a sensible and reasonably well-engineered combination that explicitly guards against identifiable reward-hacking failure modes (e.g., under-generating people, grid artifacts), and the paper is transparent about these failure modes and how each reward term mitigates them.

Strong and consistent empirical gains are reported across two benchmarks (a new DiverseHumans testset and the independent, previously published MultiHuman-TestBench) and across two backbones (Flux-Dev generalist, Krea-Dev specialist), with the method outperforming several strong open-source and proprietary baselines (Gemini-Nanobanana, GPT-Image-1) on Unique Face Accuracy and Global Identity Spread.

Thorough ablations (reward-component ablation, aggregation-function choice, reward-weight grid search, curriculum necessity) and an extensive appendix with pseudocode, dataset construction details, computational-efficiency comparisons, and qualitative visualizations support reproducibility and give insight into design choices.

Robustness across varying numbers of people and across diversity-tag conditions (implicit vs. explicit ethnicity specification) is explicitly evaluated, showing the method degrades far less than baselines as scene complexity increases.
weaknesses: The evaluation metrics (Unique Face Accuracy, Global Identity Spread, Count Accuracy) are computed with essentially the same RetinaFace+ArcFace embedding pipeline and similarity thresholds used to define the training reward. Since the model is directly optimized to reduce facial-embedding cosine similarity within and across samples, and is then evaluated by thresholding the same cosine similarity, the large reported gains are partly tautological/self-consistent rather than independent evidence of improved identity diversity as perceived by humans. This circularity is not discussed as a limitation, and no independent human study or third-party identity-verification model is used to corroborate the automated metrics.

The core technical contribution is largely a combination of existing components (GRPO/Flow-GRPO, ArcFace/RetinaFace embeddings, HPSv3 reward, curriculum learning) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea; the novelty resides mainly in the specific compositional reward design and its application to multi-human identity diversity.

Diversity is treated as uniformly desirable, but this may not be pragmatically appropriate for all group-photo contexts (e.g., family portraits, twins, or scenes where visual similarity among subjects is expected); the paper does not discuss or evaluate potential mismatches between enforced facial dissimilarity and prompt semantics implying resemblance.

Evaluation is limited to relatively small group sizes (2–7 people); scalability claims ('scalable ... solution') are not tested on larger crowds where face detection and embedding-based rewards may be less reliable, a limitation only briefly acknowledged in the appendix limitations section (occlusion, small faces, extreme poses).

The primary DiverseHumans benchmark is authored by the same team and used for both hyperparameter tuning (grid search, curriculum design) and headline results; while MultiHuman-TestBench provides an independent check, the degree of independence of the main reported numbers is limited.

No formal human perceptual study evaluates whether the generated identities are actually perceived as more distinct/realistic by people, or whether the HPS-based quality control fully avoids subtle artifacts; reliance is placed on automated proxies (HPS, MLLM-based Action score) that are themselves imperfect and, in one case (Action score with Gemini as both generator and judge), explicitly flagged by the authors as potentially misleading.

strengths: Addresses a real and practically relevant failure mode (duplicated/merged identities and miscounting in multi-human T2I generation) that is under-studied relative to single-person identity preservation.

The compositional reward design (intra-image diversity, group-wise leave-one-out diversity, count accuracy, HPS-based quality) is a reasonable and relatively novel combination for this specific problem, and the curriculum learning from simple to complex person counts is a sensible engineering choice.
Reasonably thorough ablation study (Table 2) honestly reports a failure mode (reward hacking when only group-wise diversity is used, causing undercounting), which is good scientific transparency.

Evaluation spans two datasets (a self-built DiverseHumans set and the independent MultiHuman-TestBench), showing some consistency of gains across protocols and across two base models (Flux-Dev, Krea-Dev).
Extensive appendix with pseudocode, hyperparameter grids, aggregation-function ablations, and qualitative failure visualizations, which aids understanding of design choices.
weaknesses: Severe evaluation circularity: the two headline metrics (Unique Face Accuracy and Count Accuracy, and by extension Global Identity Spread) are computed with essentially the same pipeline (RetinaFace detection + ArcFace cosine similarity, same thresholds) that is directly used as the RL training reward. Reporting near-saturated scores (e.g., 98.6% UFA) on metrics the model was explicitly optimized against is not strong evidence of genuinely improved perceptual identity diversity; it mainly shows the model has learned to satisfy the proxy it was trained on. This should at minimum be accompanied by human perceptual studies or a held-out, independently-trained identity verifier not involved in reward computation.

No human/user study anywhere in the paper or appendix to validate whether the generated group images actually look like diverse, visually distinct, natural-looking people to human observers — this is important given the stated goal is a perceptual/identity phenomenon, not just an automatic-metric target.

The DiverseHumans test set is self-constructed by the same authors using the same face-embedding philosophy as the reward, and its release/licensing status is unclear; this limits independent verifiability and increases the risk that reported superiority is partly an artifact of benchmark design matching the trained objective.

Several qualitative examples in the appendix (e.g., Fig. E.3, 'Five people in a sand mosque yard', 'Four people inside a train concourse', 'Five people in a sunflower meadow') show the DisCo-Krea outputs as tight close-up portraits of noticeably fewer clearly depicted individuals than competitor outputs, raising a concern that the model may be gaming count/diversity rewards through framing/cropping choices rather than genuinely rendering the requested number of distinct people in full scene context; this is not discussed or ruled out by the authors.

The core technical contribution is largely reward/curriculum engineering layered on an existing GRPO/Flow-GRPO RL pipeline (prior work already established GRPO for flow-matching models and diversity/quality rewards); the algorithmic novelty is incremental rather than foundational.

The diversity-forcing reward is applied uniformly without discussion of cases where real-world semantic context would naturally produce similar-looking individuals (e.g., family or twin scenarios), raising a conceptual concern about whether the reward could push toward artificial demographic diversity irrespective of scene semantics; this trade-off is not analyzed.

Reliance on RetinaFace/ArcFace means known failure modes (occlusion, small faces, extreme poses) affect both training signal and evaluation identically, which the authors acknowledge only briefly as future work rather than analyzing empirically (e.g., no failure-rate breakdown by face size/occlusion).

strengths: Clearly identifies and names an important, under-addressed failure mode in text-to-image generation—the 'identity crisis' of duplicated/merged faces and miscounted people in multi-person scenes—and provides convincing qualitative evidence (Fig. 1) that even SOTA proprietary/open models (Nanobanana, HiDream, Flux-Krea, OmniGen2) suffer from it.

The compositional reward design is sensible and well-motivated: intra-image diversity, a novel group-wise (cross-sample) diversity term using a leave-one-out counterfactual formulation, count accuracy, and an HPS-based quality term to regularize against reward hacking. The paper explicitly documents and addresses several reward-hacking failure modes (grid artifacts, under-counting) rather than glossing over them.

Extensive empirical evaluation across two benchmarks (a newly constructed DiverseHumans test set and the independent MultiHuman-TestBench), with consistent, often large improvements over both open-source and proprietary baselines in Count Accuracy, Unique Face Accuracy, and Global Identity Spread, while maintaining competitive HPS/quality scores.

Thorough ablations: progressive component ablation (Table 2), reward-weight grid search (Table E.2), aggregation-function comparison (max/mean/min, Table E.3), performance across diversity-tag conditions (Table E.1), and performance vs. number of people (Fig. 5) — this level of ablation is uncommonly thorough and strengthens the technical credibility of the design choices.

Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, training compute, pseudocode for all algorithmic components, dataset construction details, and explicit metric definitions are provided in the appendix, and the method builds on a public Flow-GRPO codebase.

Demonstrates generality by applying the framework to two structurally different base models (a generalist Flux-Dev and a specialist Krea-Dev), showing the curriculum component is especially important for the harder-to-converge specialist model.
weaknesses: Potential reward–metric circularity: the same face-detection/embedding pipeline (RetinaFace + ArcFace) used to compute the training reward is also used to compute the evaluation metrics (Count Accuracy, UFA, GIS). This creates a risk that DisCo is essentially being evaluated with (nearly) the same signal it was optimized against, which could inflate the apparent gains relative to baselines that were never exposed to this specific detector/embedding stack. The paper does not include an evaluation with an independent face/identity model to rule this out.

No human study assessing whether the increased 'identity diversity' actually looks natural/realistic to human observers, versus being an artifact of pushing ArcFace embeddings apart (e.g., exaggerated or unnatural facial variation, potential unintended shifts in perceived ethnicity/age/gender distribution to satisfy the diversity reward). The ethics/limitations section itself flags that a fairness/demographic-balance study is left to future work, which is an acknowledged but unresolved gap given the method explicitly optimizes facial dissimilarity.

The core RL infrastructure (GRPO/Flow-GRPO for flow-matching models) is adopted largely as-is from prior work (Flow-GRPO, DanceGRPO); the main novelty is confined to the reward design and a relatively simple exponential curriculum-annealing schedule, which is a incremental methodological contribution.

The DiverseHumans test set is newly authored by the paper's own team, and though corroborated with the external MultiHuman-TestBench, its prompts/tags and scoring thresholds (e.g., κ_dup=0.5 for duplicate detection, clustering threshold for GIS) are chosen by the authors, leaving some room for evaluation-protocol sensitivity that isn't stress-tested against alternative thresholds.

Comparisons against proprietary generalist systems (GPT-Image-1, Gemini-Nanobanana) may be somewhat unequal, since those systems are not optimized for strict person-count adherence or explicit ethnic/diversity tags used in the benchmark; the paper is transparent about some caveats (e.g., flagging '*' results as possibly misleading due to self-judging bias) but this reduces the strength of the 'outperforms proprietary models' claim.

Failure modes are only characterized qualitatively for heavy occlusion/extreme poses/small faces (noted in Limitations) without any quantitative breakdown of how often such failures occur or how they affect the reported metrics.

strengths: Identifies and clearly articulates a real, under-addressed failure mode ('identity crisis': duplicate/merged faces and miscounted people) in SOTA multi-human text-to-image generation, backed by convincing qualitative comparisons against very recent systems (Gemini-Nanobanana, GPT-Image-1, HiDream, Flux-Krea, OmniGen2).

Technically well-motivated method: the paper makes a non-trivial empirical observation that intra-image diversity rewards alone cause 'global diversity collapse' (duplicates migrate across samples rather than being eliminated), and addresses it with a principled group-relative counterfactual reward (leave-one-out contribution to group similarity) integrated cleanly into GRPO.

Extensive and rigorous ablations: reward component ablation (Table 2), reward-weight grid search, aggregation-function comparison (max/mean/min), curriculum-bound ablation, RL-vs-SFT comparison (isolating benefit of RL over simple best-of-N SFT), and OOD generalization to higher person counts (8-10) — this is a thorough experimental treatment rarely seen at this depth in appendices.

Goes beyond the narrow metric it optimizes: shows generalization of the diversity behavior to clothing/body-type diversity, preserved/improved GenEval2 compositional performance, and preserved fine-grained per-person attribute control (clothing/hairstyle prompts), which addresses the natural worry that RL fine-tuning for one objective could degrade general capability.

Includes a modest human preference study (25 participants, 22 pairs) that validates that the automatic face-embedding-based metrics (UFA, cosine similarity) correlate with human judgments of identity diversity, partially mitigating concerns about self-referential/circular metrics.

Reproducibility: hyperparameters, training data curation process, evaluation protocols, and pseudocode are given in detail, and the method builds on a public Flow-GRPO codebase without requiring extra annotated data.

Strong, consistent quantitative improvements across two independent benchmarks (DiverseHumans-Test, MultiHuman-TestBench) and two backbones (Flux-Dev generalist, Krea-Dev specialist), including outperforming proprietary black-box models on UFA/GIS while remaining competitive on HPS/quality.
weaknesses: Core evaluation metrics (Count Accuracy, UFA, GIS) are computed with the same RetinaFace+ArcFace pipeline used to construct the training reward, creating a risk of metric/reward circularity: the model is essentially directly optimized toward what is measured, which inflates the apparent margin over baselines that were never optimized for this specific pipeline (including proprietary models evaluated 'out of the box'). The user study helps but is small-scale (22 pairs, one baseline comparison only) and does not fully resolve this concern.

The framework's notion of 'identity diversity' as an unconditional good is not critically examined: many realistic multi-person scenes (families, siblings, twins, uniformed teams) plausibly contain individuals who look similar; the reward may push the model toward unrealistic enforced dissimilarity in such cases, and the paper does not test or discuss this failure mode explicitly, nor report any realism/naturalness metric beyond HPS.

Comparisons to proprietary end-to-end systems (Gemini-Nanobanana, GPT-Image-1) are somewhat asymmetric — these are general foundation models not fine-tuned on the paper's specific training distribution or reward, whereas DisCo is directly optimized for the exact evaluation criteria, which should temper claims of 'surpassing proprietary models.'

The training/eval pipeline depends on several hand-set thresholds (face-detection confidence η_det=0.7, duplicate-similarity κ_dup=0.5, count target matching) whose sensitivity is not analyzed; small changes in these thresholds could materially change reported metrics, and there is no robustness analysis for threshold choice.

Method is restricted to face-based identity and explicitly does not address personalization, occlusion, extreme pose, or very small faces (acknowledged as limitations), and evaluation resolution during training (512x512, 14 timesteps) versus test (1024x1024, 28 steps) introduces a train/test mismatch whose effect on results is not analyzed.

Ablation and hyperparameter search (Table 2, E.1.2) is conducted mainly on the Flux/Krea backbones at reduced epoch counts (300 vs. 480 for final results), and it is unclear how sensitive the chosen weights are to backbone/dataset choice or whether they would transfer to other flow-matching or diffusion backbones not tested.

strengths: Clearly identifies and motivates an under-addressed failure mode in modern T2I models—duplicate/merged identities and miscounted people in multi-human scenes—with compelling qualitative evidence across several recent SOTA systems (Fig. 1, Fig. 4).

The compositional reward design is thoughtfully engineered and empirically justified: the paper uncovers and demonstrates the non-obvious phenomenon that optimizing only intra-image diversity causes duplicate identities to migrate across samples rather than disappear ('global diversity collapse'), motivating the novel group-relative counterfactual (leave-one-out) cross-sample reward. This is a genuine methodological insight, not just an incremental combination of known terms.

Extensive empirical evaluation: two benchmarks (a newly introduced DiverseHumans testset and the existing MultiHuman-TestBench), two base models (generalist Flux-Dev, specialist Krea-Dev), and comparisons against strong proprietary (Gemini-Nanobanana, GPT-Image-1) and multiple open-source baselines, with consistent, sizable improvements in count accuracy, unique-face accuracy, and global identity spread.

Thorough ablation studies (reward component ablation, curriculum bound ablation, reward-weight grid search, aggregation function choice, RL vs. online-SFT comparison, OOD scaling to 8-10 people) that substantively support individual design choices rather than only reporting a final number.

Good generalization checks beyond the immediate objective: diversity gains transfer to clothing/body-type variation, GenEval2 compositional performance is preserved or improved, and fine-grained per-person compositional prompts (hairstyle/clothing) remain followable, addressing the natural worry that RL fine-tuning for one objective might degrade general capability.

A small human preference study is included to validate that the automated face-embedding-based diversity metrics correlate with human perception of identity diversity, partially addressing metric validity concerns.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed pseudocode, hyperparameters, training/evaluation dataset descriptions, and infrastructure details are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Reward and evaluation metrics (UFA, GIS, Count Accuracy) rely on the same RetinaFace+ArcFace pipeline used to compute the training reward, creating a risk of circularity/reward-hacking toward the embedding metric rather than genuine perceptual identity diversity; the user study mitigating this concern is small (22 pairs, 25 participants) and only compares against a single baseline (Flux), not the full set of competitors, limiting how conclusive it is.

The method optimizes for maximal identity dissimilarity without discussing scenarios where similarity is intentional or desirable (e.g., families, twins, team uniforms, or prompts specifying a shared ethnicity); it is unclear whether DisCo could over-diversify in ways that are unnatural or conflict with prompt intent, and this trade-off/failure mode is not analyzed.

Table 1's main results appear to be reported as point estimates without confidence intervals/variance, in contrast to Figure 5's error bars, making it harder to judge the statistical robustness of the headline comparisons against strong baselines.

Training data (30K GPT-5-captioned prompts) and the curated DiverseHumans evaluation set rely on proprietary LLM generation; it is not entirely clear whether these prompt sets will be released, which could limit exact reproducibility despite the otherwise detailed hyperparameter/algorithm documentation.

The approach is fairly resource-intensive (21 H100 GPUs, group size M=21, 13 hours per run), and while inference-time cost is shown to be unchanged, the training cost/complexity is nontrivial and not deeply contextualized against simpler alternatives beyond the single online-SFT baseline.

Some proprietary-model comparisons (e.g., Action Score using Gemini-2.0-Flash as judge when Gemini-Nanobanana is also a competitor) are flagged by the authors themselves as "possibly misleading," which is an honest disclosure but still leaves residual concern about fairness of that particular comparison.
